title: MEPs back €200 billion Horizon Europe for 2028–2034
dek: Parliament's industry and research committee wants €200 billion for the next research programme, above the Commission's €175 billion proposal.
key_facts: €200 billion in current prices (€177 billion in 2025 prices)
Capped at 10% of the relevant appropriations
Christian Ehler (EPP, DE) and René Repasi (S&D, DE)
body: The European Parliament's Committee on Industry, Research and Energy has adopted its position on Horizon Europe for 2028–2034, the next EU framework programme for research and innovation. MEPs are asking for €200 billion in current prices, equivalent to €177 billion in 2025 prices, compared with the €175 billion put forward by the Commission. They also want to rework how the programme connects to the proposed European Competitiveness Fund.

On structure, the committee wants to keep the four existing areas of activity: excellent science, competitiveness and society, innovation, and the European Research Area. Each pillar would get its own budget line, and the Commission would only be able to move up to 10% of the relevant appropriations within a pillar. The European Research Council and the European Innovation Council would receive firm budget guarantees and protection of their independence.

MEPs also propose a high-level council of at least 30 independent experts from science, industry and civil society to advise on priorities and help prepare calls for proposals. New schemes would include a 'fast track to excellence', a 'fast track to innovation', support for researchers at risk and similar measures for the social sciences, humanities and arts.

The position on the regulation passed with 67 votes in favour, 1 against and 18 abstentions; the text on the Council Decision passed with 66 in favour, 1 against and 19 abstentions, and the mandate to open negotiations with 65 in favour, 18 against and 2 abstentions. The plenary is expected to confirm the mandate, and talks with member states can only start once the Council has adopted its own position, including the overall figures for the 2028–2034 long-term budget.
why: This is not yet the budget applicants will compete for: the final figure depends on negotiations with member states over the whole long-term budget. Still, the Parliament's mandate sets the upper bound of the debate and signals what it will defend, namely separate, protected envelopes for each pillar and for the ERC and EIC. For companies and consortia, the proposed fast-track schemes and the tighter limit on moving money between pillars would make the programme more predictable to plan around. Organisations that want a say should follow the plenary vote and the Council's position over the coming months.
